content:
We're excited to share our latest paper on Lean for scientific computing and computational chemistry: LeanBET!

Code is on GitHub, paper is on arXiv.

I'm a chemical engineer who has worked a lot on adsorption - the process in which molecules from a gas or liquid "stick" onto a surface. Our earlier paper on formalizing chemical physics featured formalized derivations for the two most prominent adsorption theories: Langmuir and BET. BET is a workhorse for characterizing the surface area of materials: you have a sample of a powder with unknown surface area/gram, you measure how much nitrogen gas is adsorbed at different pressures, then do some regression and apply the BET theory to back out the surface area of the material.

While we were working on our first formalizations, a significant paper came out in my community highlighting reproducibility issues in computational implementations of BET analysis. This paper develops a Python-based community standard for BET analysis, called BETSI. Since the computation workflow for BET is rather simple, I thought this would be a good project to demonstrate possibilities for Lean in scientific computing. In this paper, we essentially re-implement BETSI in Lean, using polymorphic functions over Reals and Floats, so the program is executed over IEEE 754 Floats and theorems are proved for the Real-instantiated functions (we used the same design in LeanLJ). The executed code agrees with the Python implementation to machine precision most of the time. We're also able to successfully link our formalized derivation of the theory to the functions that are involved in the execution. I've come to think of this as "derivation-as-specification", an interesting kind of spec that might be broadly relevant for scientific computing applications. What was tougher for us, though, was needing to align many other algorithmic decisions with BETSI - the derivation itself is not sufficient to fully specify the software.
